name: Natural Questions
description: A question answering data set consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present.
creator: Google Research
citeAs: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov. 2019. Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 7, pp. 453–466.
rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Questions are sampled from queries of 8 words or more that have been issued by multiple users in a short period of time. Simple heuristics are used to filter questions from the query stream. Questions are run through the Google search engine and kept when there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. An annotator is presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair and returns a (long answer, short answer) pair.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are filtered using heuristics that either: 1) start with 'who', 'when', or 'where' directly followed by specific verb patterns; 2) start with 'who' directly followed by a verb that is not a finite form of 'be'; 3) contain multiple entities as well as an adjective, adverb, verb, or determiner; 4) contain a categorical noun phrase immediately preceded by a preposition or relative clause; 5) end with a categorical noun phrase, and do not contain a preposition or relative clause. Questions are run through the Google search engine and kept only when there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. The annotation task is divided into three conceptual stages: 1) Question Identification: Contributors determine whether the given question is good (fact-seeking, answerable with entity or explanation) or bad (ambiguous, incomprehensible, dependent on false presuppositions, opinion-seeking, or not clearly a request for factual information). 2) Long Answer Identification: For good questions, annotators select the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information for a reader to completely infer the answer to the question. Bounding boxes can be paragraphs, tables, list items, or whole lists. Alternatively, annotators mark 'no answer' if the page does not answer the question or if the information is not contained in a single allowed element. 3) Short Answer Identification: For examples with long answers, annotators select the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question. Alternatively, annotators can flag that the short answer is yes, no, or they can flag that no short answer is possible.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed using consensus judgments from four experts. Experts categorized (question, long answer passage) pairs into three categories: Correct (C) - clear beyond reasonable doubt that the answer is correct; Correct but debatable (Cd) - a reasonable person could be satisfied by the answer but could raise reasonable doubt; Wrong (W) - not convincing evidence that the answer is correct. 25-way annotations on 302 examples were collected to study human variability. The most popular long answer accounts for 83% of long answer annotations, and the two most popular long answers account for 96%. The most popular short answer accounts for 64% of all short answer annotations, and the three most popular short answers account for 90%.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Single annotations for 307,373 training examples; 5-way annotations for 7,830 development examples and 7,842 test examples; 25-way annotations on 302 examples for variability analysis
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API for part of speech tags and entity identification during question filtering
rai:dataBiases: Questions are focused on longer queries (8 words or more) as they are more complex and challenging. The data set focuses on Wikipedia as a source of factual information, which may introduce biases inherent to Wikipedia's content and style. Questions beginning with 'how to' are excluded by the filters.
rai:dataLimitations: The data set focuses on longer queries (8 words or more in length) and excludes shorter queries. Questions beginning with 'how to' are not included. The data set is limited to Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may not represent all sources of factual information on the Web. For naturally occurring questions there is often genuine ambiguity in whether or not an answer is acceptable, and there are often multiple acceptable answers. Annotators identify a long answer for 49% of examples and short answer spans or yes/no answer for 36% of examples.
rai:dataUseCases: Training: 307,373 examples with single annotations. Development/Validation: 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations. Testing: 7,842 examples with 5-way annotations (sequestered). The task is designed to be close to an end-to-end question answering application. The input to a model is a question together with an entire Wikipedia page. The target output is: 1) a long-answer (e.g., a paragraph) from the page that answers the question, or alternatively an indication that there is no answer on the page; 2) a short answer where applicable.
